summary:
Illinois stands under the national framework of the United States. A July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills places Illinois in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier, whose laws have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

Illinois bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, credit and public accommodations, effective 1 June 2006, with 'sexual orientation' defined to include gender-related identity whether or not traditionally associated with designated sex at birth. Schools must investigate bullying based on gender identity or expression, protect student privacy and train staff.

Hate-crime penalties were expanded to cover gender identity by HB 3930, passed unanimously on 16 April and 20 May 2015, signed 20 July 2015 by Governor Bruce Rauner and effective 1 January 2016; before that, coverage existed only as perceived sexual orientation. The gay and trans panic defence was repealed by SB1761, passed unanimously in June 2017, signed 25 August 2017 and effective 1 January 2018.

Gender-affirming care is protected by legislation signed 13 January 2023, effective immediately, covering care within Illinois including for individuals coming from outside Illinois to seek services. Illinois Medicaid covers reassignment surgery costs for applicants aged at least 21, and in June 2024 the Department of Human Services and the Public Health Institute of Metropolitan Chicago announced expansion through the Transgender and Gender Diverse Wellness and Equity Program.

Changing the gender marker on an Illinois birth certificate no longer requires surgery, following legislation passed 31 May 2017 (63-43 in the House, 32-22 in the Senate), signed 25 August 2017 and effective 1 January 2018. The process requires an Affidavit and Certificate of Correction Request plus a Declaration of Gender Transition or Intersex Condition by a licensed health or mental health professional, with a $15 fee. An X option has been available since July 2020, self-attestation reform passed in January-February 2023 took effect 1 July, and since 1 July 2024 persons born outside Illinois can change sex on an Illinois birth certificate. Driver's licences and state IDs are corrected upon a Gender Designation Change Form, with X available from 2024.

Single-occupancy public restrooms were designated gender-neutral by legislation passed 109-5 in the House and 53-0 in the Senate, signed July 2019 and effective 1 January 2020. Chicago's Human Rights Ordinance, as amended in 2016, provides that each person determines their own gender identity with no proof required except expression for bathroom access, and all Chicago public schools have all-gender bathrooms by signage since December 2021. A May 2023 bill permitting multi-occupancy facility use had passed both houses but awaited the governor's signature or veto.

Funeral and burial instructions may specify gender identity and preferred pronouns under HB 3552, signed 20 August 2015 and effective 1 January 2016. Des Plaines repealed its opposite-sex clothing ban in July 2021, and a 30 June 2019 executive order protects transgender students through a task force and procedures covering names, pronouns and dress codes.

Conversion therapy on minors under 18 by mental health providers was banned under the Youth Mental Health Protection Act, passed 68-43 in the House on 19 May 2015 and 34-19 in the Senate on 29 May 2015, signed 20 August 2015 and effective 1 January 2016. A federal court dismissed a pastors' suit on 15 February 2017, holding that private religious counselling is not trade or commerce.
tangentialFactors:
Illinois holds a shield or refuge law (MAP Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, data as of 27 September 2026: 'State has shield law or executive order 2023'). The law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care legal in Illinois was banned in the home state, which is directly relevant to visitors travelling from ban states. Nationally, 16 states and D.C. (38% of trans population 13+) hold shields, while 32 states and 5 territories (56%) hold none.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1 January 1962, when a new code eliminated sodomy laws, making Illinois the first state to do so; the age of consent was set at 18, lowered to 16 in 1984 and raised to 17 effective 1 January 2012. Same-sex marriage was banned by statute in 1996 under SB 1773, then legalised by statute signed 20 November 2013 by Governor Pat Quinn and effective 1 June 2014, after House approval 61-54 and Senate approval 32-21. Gender-neutral marriage certificates have been available under a July 2021 law, and 2023 repealed out-of-jurisdiction null-and-void provisions effective 2024. Civil unions have been recognised since 1 June 2011.

Discrimination on sexual orientation has been banned in employment, housing, public accommodations and credit since 1 June 2006, expanded by removal of the 15-employee loophole signed August 2019 effective 1 July 2020 after a 2018 veto. Jury-selection discrimination on sexual orientation was banned effective 1 January 2020 after unanimous passage in May 2019, and the anti-bullying law was expanded in 2014 to include sexual orientation. Hate-crime legislation since 1991 provides harsher penalties for crimes based on actual or perceived sexual orientation alongside race, religion, sex and other categories.

The Illinois Domestic Violence Act, in gender-neutral language, applies to same-sex partners sharing or having shared a dwelling or dating relationship. The state permits adoption by gay individuals or partners, including second-parent adoptions with IVF and gestational surrogacy access, and a May 2021 bill repealed the 1983 HIV infection public health law effective immediately upon governor signature.

On intersex rights, Lurie Children's Hospital in July 2020 apologised for past non-consensual infant surgeries to make genitalia appear more typically male or female and announced cessation unless medically necessary.

outOfScopeNotes:
A May 2023 multi-occupancy permissive-use restroom bill had passed both houses but awaited governor signature or veto; the inventory does not resolve whether it was signed, so the operative position on multi-occupancy facility use in Illinois is unresolved.

The inventory does not address how Illinois's shield law interacts with federal enforcement or federal funding conditions, nor whether any Illinois measure has been challenged in federal court under the current national framework.
